body:
hi there -

database identifiers can actually have a wide variety of characters in them, they just need to be quoted.

in this case it seems like we don't apply quoting as we normally do:

```
>>> print(select([func.MyFunction()]))
SELECT MyFunction() AS "MyFunction_1"

```

it's likely that it hasnt been an issue since most SQL functions are using case-insensitive names but I suppose it's possible that custom SQL functions might not.   So that's a more ordinary issue we can fix, here is a patch that can serve as the basis for the fix:

```diff
diff --git a/lib/sqlalchemy/sql/compiler.py b/lib/sqlalchemy/sql/compiler.py
index b703c59f23..a841433fb3 100644
--- a/lib/sqlalchemy/sql/compiler.py
+++ b/lib/sqlalchemy/sql/compiler.py
@@ -1073,13 +1073,32 @@ class SQLCompiler(Compiled):
         else:
             name = FUNCTIONS.get(func.__class__, None)
             if name:
+                name = (
+                    self.preparer.quote(name)
+                    if self.preparer._requires_quotes(name)
+                    else name
+                )
                 if func._has_args:
                     name += "%(expr)s"
             else:
-                name = func.name + "%(expr)s"
-            return ".".join(list(func.packagenames) + [name]) % {
-                "expr": self.function_argspec(func, **kwargs)
-            }
+                name = func.name
+                name = (
+                    self.preparer.quote(name)
+                    if self.preparer._requires_quotes(name)
+                    else name
+                )
+                name = name + "%(expr)s"
+            return ".".join(
+                [
+                    (
+                        self.preparer.quote(tok)
+                        if self.preparer._requires_quotes(tok)
+                        else tok
+                    )
+                    for tok in func.packagenames
+                ]
+                + [name]
+            ) % {"expr": self.function_argspec(func, **kwargs)}
 
     def visit_next_value_func(self, next_value, **kw):
         return self.visit_sequence(next_value.sequence)

```

so we have:

```python
from sqlalchemy import select, func

print(select([func.MyFunction()]))


print(select([func.MyPackage.MyToken.MyFunction()]))

```

```sql
SELECT "MyFunction"() AS "MyFunction_1"
SELECT "MyPackage"."MyToken"."MyFunction"() AS "MyFunction_1"

```

as for the original claim, using that special word "arbitrary", which IMO does not apply as a concern here since it is not appropriate to use untrusted user input as a python attribute name any more than it would be to use untrusted user input as the name of a SQL table (they could change it to read from private tables) or for one to send untrusted user input into the `text()` function, which also allows arbitrary SQL to be executed not to mention `connection.execute()`, the quoting routine quotes double quotes so you can't break out:

```python
from sqlalchemy import select, func

fn = getattr(func, '" delete from table "foo')
print(select([fn()]))

```

`SELECT """ delete from table ""foo"() AS """ delete from table ""foo_1"
`

> it is not appropriate to use untrusted user input as a python attribute name any more than it would be to use untrusted user input as the name of a SQL table

Yes, I agree, I would have probably ended up with a function name whitelist in any case, it just was surprising to find that I could execute sql statements that way.

Regarding "arbitrary", I'm not a native English speaker, so I may have misused it. I'll edit the original issue to avoid it.

I've tried out the patch, and it seems to fix the problem. It now correctly escapes the function name.

But I'm by no means an expert ;-)

```sql
SELECT "MAX"(id) AS "MAX_1" FROM table
```
that returns the error `function MAX(integer) does not exist`

Right, so we'd hope people are using all lower case, but also there some databases I refer to as "name normalize" databases, which are Oracle, Firebird, DB2, which represent everything as UPPERCASE, so while someone can be saying "func.max()" without issue, their source code might have a lot of calls to func.MAX() because that's how their database documents it.

```diff
@@ -3439,6 +3458,16 @@ class IdentifierPreparer(object):
             or (lc_value != value)

+    def _requires_quotes_omit_casing(self, value):
+        """Return True if the given identifier requires quoting, but
```

that should be fully compatible because anyone using special characters in a function name right now is getting invalid SQL.

>doing case sensitive quoting on function names still might be appropriate, but as it breaks compatibility we can more safely omit casing from the quoting question for now

I agree. It's probably best to save that change for a major release. As an alternative it could be enabled with an option, like a kwargs on `func` (but I'm not sure if it's possible) or when creating the engine/parser.

I've tried the latest patch and it does seem to fix the issue, keeping compatibility with upper case functions.

issue.title: Index(postgresql_using='TYPE') wraps index type in extra quotes if it's uppercase

labels.name: schema
labels.description: things related to the DDL related objects like Table, Column, CreateIndex, etc.

labels.name: easy
labels.description: a one / two  liner type of thing that anyone can do in short order. also see "fairly easy"

issue.body:
For the PostgreSQL dialect, `Index()` takes a `postgresql_using=` parameter to specify the index type. However, the generated SQL is wrong if the parameter value is uppercase:
```
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.ext import declarative
from sqlalchemy.schema import CreateTable, CreateIndex
from sqlalchemy.sql import schema, sqltypes

Base = declarative.declarative_base()

class MyTable(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'my_table'
    some_column = schema.Column(sqltypes.String(), primary_key=True)
    __table_args__ = (
        schema.Index('my_index', some_column, postgresql_using='BTREE'),
    )

engine = create_engine('postgresql://')
print(CreateTable(MyTable.__table__).compile(engine))
for index in MyTable.__table__.indexes:
    print(CreateIndex(index).compile(engine))
```

This produces the SQL:
`CREATE INDEX my_index ON my_table USING "BTREE" (some_column)`
which is invalid because `"BTREE"` is quoted.

However, if we change it to lowercase: `postgresql_using='btree'`, then it produces valid SQL.

Is the `postgresql_using` argument supposed to be case-sensitive like that?

issue.title: SQL Alchemy 1.3.0 Function Quoting fix

repository.name: datacube-core
repository.description: Open Data Cube analyses continental scale Earth Observation data through time

issue.body:
Initialize packagenames variable in SQL function classes derived from sqlalchemy GenericFunctions. Setting the packagenames list with the `agdc` string allows sqlalchemy > 1.3.0 to correctly quote the SQL function name. Possible fix for #668

### Reason for this pull request
#668 reported issues with SQL Alchemy 1.3.0 and this is potential fix to our code base to allow us to use SQL Alchemy 1.3.0.

It appears that this change https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/issues/4467 changed the way that SQL Alchemy quoted function identifiers -> the entire function name that was specified in our `CommonTimestamp` and `Float8Range` classes was quoted (`"agdc.common_timestamp"`) which is invalid in psql.

### Proposed changes
- Set the `packagenames` variable of the `CommonTimestamp` and `Float8Range` classes which are derived from `sqlalchemy.sql.functions.GenericFunction`. Setting this member variable means that SQLAlchemy will quote `"agdc"` and `"common_timestamp"` separately instead of together (i.e. `"agdc"."common_timestamp"`)

 - [ ] Closes #668
 - [ ] Tests added / passed
 - [ ] Fully documented, including `docs/about/whats_new.rst` for all changes

issue.title: GenericFunction register is case-sensitive
issue.body:
The `GenericFunction` instances are registered in `sqlalchemy.sql.functions._register`, which is a `collections.defaultdict(dict)`. The `sqlalchemy.sql.functions.func()` function uses the `get()` method to retrieved registered functions, which means that the search is case-sensitive.

This case-sensitivity can have some drawbacks, e.g.:

```python
from sqlalchemy import func
from sqlalchemy.sql.functions import GenericFunction
from sqlalchemy.types import Text, Integer

class CaseSensitiveFunc(GenericFunction):
    type = Text

class CaseInsensitiveFunc(GenericFunction):
    type = Integer

print(func.CaseSensitiveFunc().type, func.CaseInsensitiveFunc().type)  # Out: (Text(), Integer())
print(func.CaSeSeNsItIveFuNc().type, func.CaSeInSeNsItIveFuNc().type)  # Out: (NullType(), NullType())
```
In this example, the `GenericFunction(s)` are not retrieved by the `sqlalchemy.sql.functions.func()` function when their letter case is not exactly the same as in their definitions. So in this case, they are just sent to the DBMS as they are and the DBMS silently interpret them without considering the letter case, which can lead to some weird bugs (see here for example: https://github.com/geoalchemy/geoalchemy2/issues/215).

Some simple changes in `sqlalchemy.sql.functions` could add the possibility to register a `GenericFunction` without being case-sensitive. In this case we would have the following:

```python
from sqlalchemy import func
from sqlalchemy.sql.functions import GenericFunction
from sqlalchemy.types import Text, Integer

class CaseSensitiveFunc(GenericFunction):
    type = Text
    case_sensitive = True

class CaseInsensitiveFunc(GenericFunction):
    type = Integer
    case_sensitive = False

print(func.CaseSensitiveFunc().type, func.CaseInsensitiveFunc().type)  # Out: (Text(), Integer())
print(func.CaSeSeNsItIveFuNc().type, func.CaSeInSeNsItIveFuNc().type)  # Out: (NullType(), Integer())
```

Here the case-insensitive function is retrieved by `sqlalchemy.sql.functions.func()`.

issue.title: quoted name is not applied to function name even when specified

labels.name: use case
labels.description: not really a feature or a bug; can be support for new DB features or user use cases not anticipated

issue.body:
There is one error when moving from 1.2.8 to 1.3.12 version.

I defined custom GenericFunction like this:

```python
class CustomFunction(GenericFunction): 
      type = Boolean 
      package = 'pack' 
      name = '"CustomFunction"' 
      identifier = 'CustomFunction'
```

When I used it with 1.2.8 version all was right, but when I use it
with 1.3.12 I get this error:
```postgresql
function "CustomFunction"(bigint) does not exist
```

I look at generated sql code and see following:

```postgresql
 SELECT ...,  """CustomFunction"""("columnName")  \nFROM ...
```

SQLAlchemy quotes already quoted name. I tried to find the reasons of this behaviour
and it seems it's in the `compiler.py` module. In particular, in the methods `requires_quotes` and `quote_identifier` of `IdentifierPreparer` class. They don't check if the name already has quotes.

In situation when name is without quotes, but in camel case, it converts name to lower case.

P.S. I use that GenericFunction definition when I need to construct dynamic query which
should contain calling of stored procedure in `select` section. For example:

```python
...
query = select([ 
    Table.c.column, 
    func.pack.CustomFunction(Table.c.column) ])

# code with conditions for adding relevant where clauses, like
# if condition:
#    query = query.where(...) 
...
``` 

Best regards.
